newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Barak leads Labour, aims to beat Netanyahu.
newsitem.headline: Barak leads Labour, aims to beat Netanyahu.

text.p: Former army chief Ehud Barak, triumphant in a contest for the leadership of Israel's opposition Labour party, vowed on Wednesday to push for early elections to oust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

"We'll do our best to make it a little bit earlier, maybe a year or two earlier," Barak told Reuters when asked if he would push for early elections as he waded through a jubiliant crowd at Labour party headquarters in Tel Aviv.
Israel's next general election is set for 2000.
"I wish all the candidates success and hope Labour voters pick an opposition leader who will remain such for many years," Netanyahu had said on Tuesday ahead of the Labour primary.
Hundreds of supporters greeted Barak, 55, at his offices near Tel Aviv after exit polls pointed to a landslide victory, chanting "Look who's coming, it's the next prime minister".
"This is a first step towards hope, the first step towards renewal, the first step on the path to victory which will return us to the leadership of this country," Barak said.
The Labour primary was a milestone contest that marked a passing of the political torch from former prime minister Shimon Peres, 73, and his slain predecessor, Yitzhak Rabin.

Netanyahu edged out Peres in an upset election victory in 1996, in part by characterising the Nobel peace laureate as soft on security. Opinion polls have shown Barak neck and neck with Netanyahu, 47, whose first year in office has been battered by peacemaking crises and allegations of corruption.
About 70 percent of the 167,000 registered Labour members cast ballots, Labour party election chairman Eli Dayan said.
With 61 percent of the ballots counted, Barak had 51 percent of the vote compared with 28 percent for Beilin, an architect of Labour peace policies and Peres's protege.

Candidate Shlomo Ben-Ami, 53, a Moroccan-born novice politician with roots both in academia and among the disadvantaged, came in third with 15 percent of the vote. Ephraim Sneh, 52, a physician and brigadier general before he served Rabin and Peres as health minister, received six percent.
At Labour headquarters, the four contenders joined hands for the cameras in a show of solidarity against Netanyahu.

"I want to wish Ehud Barak success...first of all to lead the Labour party, afterward to lead the opposition and after that to lead the government of Israel, I very much hope as soon as possible," Beilin said standing beside Barak.
"We are working together as one movement opposite another camp that does not want peace, that does not believe in equality, that does not believe in social justice."
The heavily favoured Barak has cast himself as heir to Rabin's warrior-turned-peacemaker mantle. He stands to become only the third Labour party leader since 1973.
Barak vowed to work with the other candidates, declaring: "We are all one camp".

Barak joined Labour two years ago after shedding the uniform of Israel's most decorated soldier. Long before entering public life, Barak was a near-legendary military figure, at one point serving as Netanyahu's commander in an elite commando unit.
"I congratulated Ehud on his victory and I congratulated Yossi on his results...Now we must move forward," Peres said.
Rabin's widow beamed at Labour party headquarters even as a tearful party activist, remembering her husband, embraced her.
"Besides respecting him and believing in his intellectual capacity, I voted for him because I see him as the winner and I want Labour to win, win, win," Leah Rabin told reporters.
